title: On Fate
author: Antonius Veritas
summary: This installment of The Stoic Workbook examines the Stoic doctrine of fate through Cleanthes' prayer and the ancient image of a dog tied to a moving cart. The author argues that the dog has real freedom within limits, and that resisting the cart's direction only leads to being dragged, while moving with it turns constraint into freedom. He applies the image to job loss, betrayal, grief, and aging, allowing time to grieve and seek justice but insisting that eventually one must act within the world that now exists. The piece then pushes further with Marcus Aurelius, who asked himself to love what happens as material woven into the pattern of one's own life. It closes with a series of Socratic questions that press the reader to distinguish acceptance of unchangeable facts from mere passivity or lowered ambition.
points: The dog-and-cart image frames freedom as choosing how to move within limits one cannot control rather than escaping them.
The author permits grief, justice, and rebuilding, but warns that bargaining with reality eventually becomes a refusal to move forward.
Marcus Aurelius is presented as going beyond acceptance toward loving adversity as necessary material for one's particular life.
The closing questions explicitly test whether acceptance is being used as an excuse for laziness or abandoned ambition.
quotes: Early Stoics used the idea of a dog tied to a cart to illustrate how much power the invincible forces of the universe have over humans and what's in our power in this interesting situation.
But if it chooses to continue just as the cart does, it'll own the journey- constraint becomes freedom.
You can't negotiate with aging, go back in time to change yesterday's mistake, or wish death, illness, work and bad weather away.
You can slow down to cry, to grieve, to prevent bitter from turning sour, seek justice, leave and rebuild- but after some time we have to keep going with and from the world that now exists.

What would happen if you learned to regard the difficult and unwanted parts of life as necessary material to your particular existence- as something to learn from, work with to build your quirks, and create a beautiful life with?

Should you accept a mediocre life and castrate your ambition just because fate is leading you? If not, how would you differentiate between accepting the facts you can't change from simply being lazy and unbothered to do your best in the right strategy?
